title: Sargon of Akkad
wiki_lead:
Sargon of Akkad (; Akkadian: 𒊬𒊒𒄀, romanized: Šarrugi; died c. 2279 BC), also known as Sargon the Great, was the founder of the Akkadian Empire (also labelled 'Sargonic', after him), known for his conquests of the Sumerian city-states, around 2300 BC. He is sometimes identified as the first person in recorded history to rule over an empire. The dates of his reign, which are uncertain, are often estimated to be between 2334 and 2279 BC, but a more recent proposal places it in the period from 2316 to 2277 BC.
His reign remains relatively poorly understood, as historians have only a few commemorative inscriptions that can be reliably dated to Sargon’s reign (most of which are known from later copies) and few archives from his time. The literary texts written after Sargon’s death with the aim of glorifying him undoubtedly contain a core of historical truth, but it is difficult to separate fact from fiction. He was a ruler of the small city of Akkad, located in central Mesopotamia, which lay in the shadow of its most-powerful neighbor, Kish. Under circumstances that remain unclear, Sargon managed to overthrow the established order and established himself as the ruler of the northern part of Lower Mesopotamia at the end of the 24th century B.C. He then confronted and defeated Lugal-zage-si, the king of Uruk, who ruled the southern part of that same region—the land of Sumer—which subsequently came under Akkadian control. He then undertook successful military expeditions toward the Iranian Plateau to the east (notably into Elam) and toward Syria to the west (Mari), though he did not incorporate these territories into his kingdom. His reign clearly marked a turning point in the history of this region, especially since his immediate successors would carry on his legacy for at least a century, thereby establishing what is generally considered the first 'imperial' experiment in history.
Sargon’s reign also made a strong impression on his contemporaries, and his memory has been preserved by future generations of Mesopotamian civilization, who have woven legends about him, some of them based at least in some part on feats he actually accomplished, but with a major part of invention. Stories have thus been told about his birth, his rise to power, and some of his military campaigns. Sargon of Akkad has thus become one of the major figures in Mesopotamian history, generally regarded as the archetype of the conquering ruler.

Stories have thus been told about his birth, his rise to power, and some of his military campaigns. Sargon of Akkad has thus become one of the major figures in Mesopotamian history, generally regarded as the archetype of the conquering ruler.


Name

The name Sargon is in Old Akkadian, the language of the Akkadian period, śarru(m)-kēn. In the cuneiform script of the time, it is written as śar-ru-GI or šar-ru-Gi.
In subsequent periods, the Akkadian name was normalized as either Šarru-ukīn or Šarru-kēn. The name's cuneiform spelling is variously LUGAL-ú-kin, 
šar-ru-gen6, šar-ru-ki-in, šar-ru-um-ki-in. 
In Old Babylonian tablets relating the legends of Sargon, his name is transcribed as 𒊬𒊒𒌝𒄀𒅔 (Šar-ru-um-ki-in).
In Late Assyrian references, the name is mostly spelled as LUGAL-GI.NA or LUGAL-GIN, i.e. identical to the name of the Neo-Assyrian king Sargon II.
The spelling Sargon is derived from the single mention of the name (in reference to Sargon II) in the Hebrew Bible, as סַרְגוֹן, in Isaiah 20:1.
The first element in the name is šarru, the Akkadian (East Semitic) for "king" (cf. Hebrew śar שַׂר). Until Sargon, this term does not seem to have been commonly used to form personal names in Akkadian. Its Sumerian equivalent, lugal, was however often used in personal names. The second element is derived either from the verb kânu "to confirm, establish" (cognate to Hebrew kūn כּוּן), or from the related adjective kēnu "authentic, legitimate".; other translations are "true," "reliable," "just," "honest," "decent," "loyal," "correct," "regular," "firm (in place)," etc.
Who is the 'King' referred to by this name? According to some, it is Sargon himself. This would mean that he changed his name upon assuming power, adopting what is known as a “throne name,” which would the be different from his birth name. However, this practice is not attested for this period and did not become common in Mesopotamia until a millennium later. On the other hand, if Sargon had borne the same name since birth, then the “King” referred to in the name would refer to the ruler who reigned at the time of his birth, seeking to bestow his blessing upon him. This practice is common in Akkadian personal names from later periods. It has also been suggested that the “King” is in fact a deity.
A possible interpretation of the reading Šarru-ukīn is "the king has established (stability)" or "he [the god] has established the king". Such a name would however be unusual; other names in -ukīn always include both a subject and an object, as in Šamaš-šuma-ukīn "Shamash has established an heir". The reading Šarru-kēn has been interpreted adjectivally, as "the king is established; legitimate", expanded as a phrase šarrum ki(e)num. The interpretation “Legitimate king” amounts to acknowledging that this is a programmatic "throne name", intended to legitimize the king's position, in an effort to make people forget that he is a usurper. If it is a birth name, it could mean “the King is true (to his word)”, or “the King is just.”
The terms "Pre-Sargonic" and "Post-Sargonic" were used in Assyriology based on the chronologies of Nabonidus before the historical existence of Sargon of Akkad was confirmed. 
The form Šarru-ukīn was known from the Assyrian Sargon Legend discovered in 1867 in Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh.
A contemporary reference to Sargon thought to have been found on the cylinder seal of Ibni-sharru, a high-ranking official serving under Sargon. Joachim Menant published a description of this seal in 1877, reading the king's name as Shegani-shar-lukh, and did not yet identify it with "Sargon the Elder" (who was identified with the Old Assyrian king Sargon I).
In 1883, the British Museum acquired the "mace-head of Shar-Gani-sharri", a votive gift deposited at the temple of Shamash in Sippar. This "Shar-Gani" was identified with the Sargon of Agade of Assyrian legend.
The identification of "Shar-Gani-sharri" with Sargon was recognised as mistaken in the 1910s. Shar-Gani-sharri (Shar-Kali-Sharri) is, in fact, Sargon's great-grandson, the successor of Naram-Sin.
It is not entirely clear whether the Neo-Assyrian king Sargon II was directly named for Sargon of Akkad, as there is some uncertainty whether his name should be rendered Šarru-ukīn or as Šarru-kēn(u).


Sources
 


Contemporary texts
Few primary sources dating from the time of Sargon's reign are known. These include some original royal inscriptions written on monuments unearthed at archaeological sites, especially Susa (ancient Elam, present-day Iran) where they were taken as booty more than a millennium after Sargon's reign. Several of his inscriptions were also copied by scribes onto cuneiform tablets after his death, particularly during the early 2nd millennium BC. This applies especially to those made on monuments displayed at Nippur, in the courtyard of the temple of Enlil, which were still present half a millennium after they were written (and which have since disappeared). They contain information about his military conquests, but do not present detailed accounts of the events. The copy tablets also include information about the visual aspect of the monuments on which the texts were inscribed (type, location of the inscriptions, images).
Among the texts commemorating the king's accomplishments are also year names: following a practice that became widespread at this time to differentiate between years, a year was given a name in reference to a major event that occurred the previous year. These names are used to date some administrative documents, and this is how historians generally identify them. This can be very useful for reconstructing the sequence of events of a reign, provided that all (or at least most) of a king's year names are known and that it is possible to put them in order. However, this is not the case for Sargon: only four year names are known for his reign (which is credited with at least 40 years). They all commemorate military victories, which are also mentioned in royal inscriptions.
Also dating from the reign of Sargon are archival documents, cuneiform tablets, mostly from Adab, Umma and Nippur.


Pseudo-historical texts
Written sources composed after Sargon's reign attest to the emergence of a legendary, or 'pseudo-historical', tradition rewriting his accomplishments or elaborating new ones (this type of text also refers to his grandson Naram-Sin). They primarily provide information about their time of composition, particularly regarding the ideology of kingship. Their usefulness in reconstructing the history of the Akkadian Empire is debated. It has been noted that these traditions have even influenced the image of this period among modern historians, who have often tended to rely too heavily on them to study the reigns of Akkadian kings, or even to adopt, without the necessary critical distance, the 'heroic' and 'imperial' vision of the period they convey. It is now recognized that it is difficult, but not necessarily impossible, to regard them as reliable historical sources and use them to reconstruct Sargon's reign. At least in some cases they are based on some truth, since some of these texts are inspired by commemorative inscriptions. But they also include a large number of imaginary events invented centuries after his death. Some historians ignore them when it comes to reconstructing the history of the Akkadian Empire, while others consider it necessary to continue using them, but with caution.


Non-textual sources

Non-textual sources are very few. Among the sculptures datable to the early Akkadian period by their style, only one fragmentary stela bears an inscription in the name of Sargon. One or two others may date from his reign, but do not mention the king that would confirm indeed belong to that period. 
In archaeology, the beginning of the Akkadian period (the reign of Sargon and his two successors Rimush and Manishtushu) cannot be distinguished from the end of the Early Dynastic period based on material criteria in the stratigraphic levels of Mesopotamian sites. Without epigraphic finds, it is impossible to date them more precisely.


Chronology
Various copies of the Sumerian King List give the duration of his reign as either 40 or 54–56 years. Only a few contemporary inscriptions relating to Sargon exist, though there are a number of Old Babylonian period texts that purport to be copies of earlier inscriptions of Sargon. It is impossible to confirm this due to a lack of additional sources. 
Since it is unknown when he ascended the throne, and given the uncertainty regarding the length of his reign, the dates of his reign in absolute years proposed by historians are only approximate: c. 2334-2279 BC, 2324-2285 BC, or 2316-2277 BC in the middle chronology.
It is unknown at what point in his reign the events mentioned in the king's inscriptions took place, notably his victory against Lugal-zage-si, which is a pivotal moment.


Year names
While various copies of the Sumerian king list and later Babylonian chronicles credit Sargon with a reign length ranging from 34 to 56 years, dated documents have been found for only four different year-names of his actual reign. The names of these four years describe his campaigns against Elam, Mari, Simurrum, and Uru'a/Arawa (in western Elam).

Year in which Sargon went to Simurrum
Year in which Sargon destroyed Uru'a/Arawa (in westernmost portion of Elam)
Year in which Sargon destroyed Elam
Year in which Mari was destroyed


Family

Like the other kings of the Akkadian dynasty, Sargon does not mention his father in his inscriptions. His parentage  therefore remain unknown. According to the Sumerian Sargon Legend, written long after his death, his father was a man named La’ipum. The name of Sargon's main wife, Queen
grok_lead: Sargon of Akkad (Akkadian: Å arru-kin (ð¬ðð), meaning "true king"), also known as Sargon the Great, was the founder and first ruler of the Akkadian Empire, reigning approximately 2334â2279 BCE and establishing the world's earliest known multi-national empire through conquest of Sumerian city-states in southern Mesopotamia. Rising from likely low origins as a cupbearer or administrator in the northern Mesopotamian city of Kish, Sargon overthrew local rulers and systematically subdued independent Sumerian polities such as Uruk, Ur, and Lagash, integrating their territories into a centralized Akkadian domain centered on the newly founded capital of Akkad. His military campaigns, documented in royal inscriptions and supported by archaeological evidence of Akkadian-style artifacts across conquered regions, extended Akkadian influence beyond Mesopotamia to the Persian Gulf, eastern Syria, and possibly Anatolia, involving innovations like a standing professional army of 5,400 soldiers and logistical reforms for sustained warfare. Sargon promoted administrative standardization, including uniform weights, measures, and the Akkadian language as a lingua franca, while appointing loyal officials and his daughter Enheduanna as high priestess of Inanna in Ur to legitimize rule through religious and cultural ties. These efforts marked a shift from city-state autonomy to imperial governance, influencing subsequent Near Eastern empires despite the empire's relatively short duration before collapse under his successors. Later propagandistic texts, such as the Legend of Sargon, embellish his biography with motifs of divine favor and humble birth, but core historical details derive from contemporary inscriptions and material remains rather than unverified folklore.
